title: My Fiancé Insisted We Marry on October 17. Then a Courthouse Clerk Told Me That Date Had Been Used Before (PART 2)

blocks.text: I didn't understand. The woman's name was Megan. Megan Cole. Same first name as me, Megan, different last name. She asked me to meet her at a coffee shop the next day. She brought a folder.

Inside was a newspaper clipping from 2014. A young woman named Megan Hart, twenty-two, Ryan's college girlfriend, had died in a car accident on October 16. They'd been planning to elope the next day, October 17, at her grandparents' farmhouse outside Savannah.
"He never got over it," Megan Cole said. "I didn't know any of this when we met. He was charming and attentive. He wanted to marry fast. On October 17."

On their wedding night, he drove her to the farmhouse. Megan Hart's family had sold it years before, but Ryan had bought it quietly. Inside, the bedroom was arranged like a shrine: her photos, her clothes in the closet, a wedding dress on a hanger.
He asked his new wife to put on the dress. He called her by her name, which was also his wife's name, but he said it differently, softer, like he was talking to someone else.

"He never hurt me," she said. "He wasn't violent. But every October 17, he wanted me to go back there and be her. Wear her perfume. Read her letters out loud. When I refused, he'd go silent for weeks. I realized I wasn't married to him. I was standing in for someone."
She'd filed for an annulment on the grounds that he'd married her under false pretenses. The judge sealed the records at her request because she didn't want her story in the paper.
I went home and asked Ryan, very calmly, if he'd ever loved anyone named Megan before me. He went pale.

Then he started crying, and he told me everything. The accident. The farmhouse. The dress. He said he'd been sure that this time it would be different. That I was the one who would finally make October 17 a happy day again.

I asked him to take me to the farmhouse. He did. The room was exactly as Megan Cole described. On the dresser was a framed photo of a young woman with my haircut. My haircut. The one he'd suggested I try last spring.
I took off my engagement ring and set it on the dresser beside her picture.
I didn't hate him. I still don't. He'd been grieving for twelve years and nobody had ever helped him do it. I told him I would not marry him, and that I hoped he would get real help.
His sister called me a week later to say he'd checked himself into a grief counseling program and finally agreed to sell the farmhouse.
October 17 came and went this year. I spent it at a beach with my friends, including, of all people, Megan Cole. We've become close. We joke that we're the founding members of a very small club.

Last week, Ryan's sister sent me a message: he'd taken the dress to Megan Hart's mother, who hadn't known it still existed. They sat together and cried and talked about her for hours. Then he drove away and didn't go back.
I think that might have been his real wedding day. The day he finally let her go.
